title: Carciofi alla giudia
subtitle: Roman Jewish fried artichokes
excerpt: Whole small artichokes, trimmed, pressed open, and twice-fried in olive oil until the outer leaves are crunchy like crisps and the heart is soft and yielding. The signature dish of the Jewish Ghetto in Rome.
sourceNotes: Carciofi alla giudia is one of the defining dishes of Roman Jewish cooking. It is documented extensively in Edda Servi Machlin's The Classic Cuisine of the Italian Jews (1981) and in Ada Boni's Il Talismano della Felicità (1929). The dish is listed as a traditional Roman Jewish recipe in the official records of the Jewish community of Rome and is considered a protected element of Roman gastronomy. Its origins go back at least to the sixteenth century in the Roman Ghetto.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The first fry can be done 2 hours ahead; hold the artichokes at room temperature and do the second fry just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: The large, round, nearly thornless artichoke variety grown in Lazio and used in Roman cooking. The mammola variety is preferred for carciofi alla giudia because of its size and the absence of thorns on its leaves. If unavailable, use any firm, fresh globe artichoke and remove the inner choke carefully.

content.text: Carciofi alla giudia is the kind of dish that makes people stop eating and pay attention. The outer leaves, fanned open and fried crisp, taste like artichoke-flavoured crisps. The heart, cooked through in the first fry, is soft, buttery, and grassy. The whole artichoke, golden and spread on the plate like a flower, looks extraordinary. The method is straightforward; the skill is in the trimming, which takes practice.

content.text: Fill a large bowl with cold water and squeeze in the juice of one lemon. Have a peeled lemon half to hand to rub the cut surfaces as you work.

Snap off the tough outer leaves until you reach the pale, tender inner leaves. Cut the top third off the artichoke with a sharp knife. Trim the base and peel the stem, leaving 3 to 4 cm attached. Rub cut surfaces immediately with the lemon half. Drop the trimmed artichoke into the acidulated water. Repeat with all artichokes.

Dry the artichokes very thoroughly. Heat the oil in a large, deep, heavy pan to 160°C. Add the artichokes (they should be submerged, or nearly so) and cook for 12 to 15 minutes until completely tender when pierced in the heart with a skewer. Lift out and drain. While still hot, use the back of a spoon or your fingers (carefully) to press the leaves outward, fanning them open like a flower.

Raise the oil to 180°C. Return the artichokes, pressed-side down, and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the outer leaves are golden, crisp, and starting to separate. They will open further and crisp dramatically. Lift out and drain on kitchen paper. Season immediately with sea salt flakes and a squeeze of lemon. Serve at once.

items.cause: Artichokes not dried before frying, or second-fry oil not hot enough
items.fix: Dry very thoroughly after trimming and acidulated soaking. The second fry at 180°C is what crisps the leaves.

items.symptom: Heart is hard and uncooked after 15 minutes first fry
items.cause: Artichokes too large or oil temperature too high, cooking the outside before the inside
items.fix: Lower the oil temperature to 155°C and cook longer. Large artichokes may need up to 20 minutes for the first fry.

content.text: Carciofi alla giudia is one of the defining dishes of Roman Jewish cooking. This cuisine developed in the closed world of the Roman Ghetto over nearly four centuries and has given Rome some of its most distinctive recipes. The dish appears in Rome every spring when the local mammola artichokes come into season. Eating it in the restaurants of the Ghetto in the Rione Sant'Angelo is one of the most characteristically Roman experiences in Italian food. Outside Rome it is difficult to find. It requires the right artichokes at the right moment: too young and they have no heart, too old and the leaves are too tough to eat.
